## The same six notes, three neighbourhoods

A melody can have every interval right and still fail, because nobody told it
where to live. Pack close notes down at the bottom of the piano and they smear
into one heavy mass. Take the identical shape up four octaves and it turns
thin and wiry. Pitch class tells you which family each note belongs to.
A playable part also needs a band of frequency to occupy.

*Register* is that band. The program treats each root as a base address and
adds the same six offsets at C2, C4 and C6. Nothing about the contour changes,
so you can follow one shape through three regions of the instrument. Each root
gets its own synth in the first run, which makes it a survey of three plausible
roles; the first edit strips that away and leaves register on its own.

Listen for three specific things: how easily you can separate one note from the
next, how much weight the phrase carries, and how sharp each attack is. All
three move with register before any second part is competing for room.

## Hear one contour move house

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 92

offsets = [0, 3, 5, 7, 5, 2]
parts = [
  {root: note(:c2), synth: :fm, amp: 0.7},
  {root: note(:c4), synth: :pluck, amp: 0.8},
  {root: note(:c6), synth: :blade, amp: 0.55}
]

parts.each do |part|
  use_synth part[:synth]
  offsets.each do |offset|
    play part[:root] + offset, amp: part[:amp], release: 0.35
    sleep 0.5
  end
  sleep 1
end
```

The low `:fm` phrase arrives with mass, and its neighbouring pitches fight each
other for room. In the middle, `:pluck` puts the contour right in front of you,
one attack at a time. Up at C6, `:blade` shows you edge, and the same numeric
leaps read as wider gaps. Your speakers have a say in all of this, especially
at the bottom.

## Hold the timbre still

1. Give all three entries `:pluck` and one shared amplitude. Now timbre is
   fixed, so whatever remains of the weight, clarity and attack differences
   belongs to register alone. Run it before you read the next variation: how
   much of what you heard the first time survives?

2. Restore the original synths, then move the low phrase up one octave with its
   sound untouched. Compare C2 against C3 directly and mark the point where
   individual pitches become traceable again.

3. Restore the three roots and play the lines at the same time, amplitudes
   pulled down first. One line goes missing before the others. Try moving that
   line by an octave and see whether separation comes back without a single
   offset changing.

## Offsets are relative addresses

The offsets behave like relative addresses and each root supplies the base
pointer. Add `[0, 3, 5, 7, 5, 2]` to a new root and the phrase relocates with
its internal steps intact. That's the argument for keeping score data relative
until a part is handed its range.

Octave transposition connects this back to [Lesson 8](08-twelve-pitch-classes.qmd) exactly. Adding twelve
changes the MIDI address and leaves the remainder modulo twelve alone. The C2
phrase and the C6 phrase run the same class pattern in frequency bands four
octaves apart. One representation proves they're the same thing; the other
remembers where each one sits.

Location does more than raise or lower a line. Low notes spread energy across a
wide band and mask whatever is near them, which is why a close-spaced chord
transplanted downward turns from clarity into rumble. High notes expose
transients and noise that blended away lower down. Wide spacing buys legibility
in the bass; close spacing survives easily up top.

Every synth has a working range, whatever note numbers Sonic Pi will accept.
Samples, filters and envelopes all respond differently across the spectrum.
Treat that range as something you observed in an arrangement, not as a fact
declared by the synth's name.

Keeping root, synth and amplitude together in one hash makes the whole role
assignment inspectable, and lets you change one field across all three entries
at once. Here's the habit worth forming: when a texture goes muddy, read the
register addresses before you touch the faders. Turning a line up usually
increases the masking. Moving it often solves the real conflict.

[Lesson 10](10-sharps-flats-why-spelling-sound.qmd) finds another reason a MIDI integer isn't the whole story. Register
lives in the full address. Harmonic intent can live in a note's spelling, and
two spellings share one address.

## Chart where each synth actually lives

Pick three synths and run each one at C2, C4 and C6 with the same offsets,
envelope and a moderate amplitude. For each synth, write down the lowest and
highest root where you can still trace the whole contour, plus one concrete
observation: "attacks merge below C3", or "upper notes expose filter noise".

Then use your own chart to build a three-part arrangement with a bass, a middle
and a high phrase. Play them together and follow each line in turn. When one
vanishes, change its octave before you change its notes or its level. By the
end you should be able to say why every part sits where it sits.
